description: Subdomain Versioning allows APIs to be versioned based on the subdomain used in the request, enabling different versions of the API to be served from different subdomains.
Hybrid Versioning Strategy combines multiple versioning techniques, such as URI versioning and header versioning, to provide flexibility in API version management.
Database Schema Versioning involves managing changes to the database schema in a way that is compatible with different API versions, ensuring data integrity across versions.
Client-Side Version Control allows clients to specify which version of the API they wish to interact with, often through request headers or query parameters.
Feature Flag Versioning uses feature flags to control the availability of certain features in different API versions, allowing for gradual rollouts and testing.
API Gateway Versioning Support refers to the capabilities of API gateways to manage and route requests to different API versions based on versioning rules.
Timestamp Versioning involves using timestamps to indicate the version of the API, allowing clients to request the API state as of a specific time.
Client-Driven Versioning allows clients to dictate the version of the API they wish to use, often through custom headers or URL parameters.
Rollback Versioning provides mechanisms to revert to a previous version of the API in case of issues with the current version, ensuring stability.
Granular Versioning allows for versioning at a more detailed level, such as individual endpoints or features, rather than at the API level as a whole.
Versioning GraphQL APIs involves strategies specific to GraphQL, such as using fields or types to manage different versions of the API schema.
Microservice Versioning addresses the challenges of versioning APIs in a microservices architecture, where multiple services may depend on different API versions.
Dynamic Versioning allows the API to adapt its version based on runtime conditions or client requests, providing a flexible approach to version management.
Contract Versioning focuses on maintaining and evolving the contracts (schemas) between clients and APIs, ensuring compatibility across versions.
Versioning Feedback Loops involve mechanisms for gathering feedback from users about different API versions to inform future development and versioning strategies.
Backward Compatibility Strategies are approaches to ensure that new versions of the API do not break existing clients, maintaining compatibility with older versions.
Branching Versioning Strategy involves creating branches in the API development process to manage different versions concurrently, allowing for parallel development.
API Composition Versioning refers to strategies for managing versions in APIs that aggregate multiple services, ensuring that the composition remains stable across versions.
Service Mesh Versioning involves managing API versions within a service mesh architecture, allowing for fine-grained control over traffic routing and version management.
Sandbox Versioning provides a testing environment where different versions of the API can be deployed and tested without affecting production systems.
Versioned API Documentation Tools are tools designed to help document different versions of an API, ensuring that users have access to the correct documentation for the version they are using.
Versioning for Rate Limiting involves strategies for applying rate limits based on API versions, ensuring that different versions can have different usage policies.
User Role-Based Versioning allows different API versions to be served based on the user's role, providing tailored experiences for different user types.
Versioning for A/B Testing involves strategies for serving different API versions to different user segments for testing purposes, allowing for data-driven decisions on API changes.
Environment-Specific Versioning allows different API versions to be deployed in different environments (e.g., development, staging, production), facilitating testing and deployment.

The Leaky Bucket Algorithm is a rate limiting algorithm that allows requests to be processed at a constant rate, smoothing out bursts of traffic by queuing excess requests.

Using Redis as a backend to store request counts and timestamps for implementing distributed rate limiting across multiple servers.
The Sliding Window Algorithm is a rate limiting technique that allows for more flexible request management by considering a time window for requests.
Concurrent Request Limits refer to the maximum number of simultaneous requests that can be processed for a user or IP address, helping to manage server load.
IP-based Rate Limiting restricts the number of requests a single IP address can make to an API, helping to prevent abuse and ensure fair usage.
Quota Management involves tracking and controlling the number of requests made by users or applications to ensure they stay within predefined limits.
Burst Rate Control is a technique used to manage sudden spikes in traffic by allowing a temporary increase in request limits before enforcing stricter controls.
Django Ratelimit Middleware is a middleware component that applies rate limiting rules to incoming requests before they reach the view layer.
Third-Party Rate Limiting Services are external services that provide rate limiting capabilities, allowing developers to offload this responsibility from their own infrastructure.
Integrating Cache with Rate Limiting involves using caching mechanisms to store request counts and timestamps, improving performance and reducing database load.
Token Bucket with Burst Capacity is a rate limiting strategy that allows for a burst of requests up to a certain limit, after which requests are processed at a steady rate.
Rate Limiting with Django Channels involves applying rate limiting strategies to WebSocket connections, ensuring that real-time communication remains efficient and manageable.
